1.pericope_label: Why do ye look one upon another? Get you down thither, and buy for us

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the scene in the second rainless season, when flocks languish and household retainers grow enfeebled and begin to die of the low fever that follows famine, explains how the report reached Canaan by the caravan trade between Palestine and Egypt, and turns the numbers over: either the households had been thinned by famine or each brother took servants, and since flocks and servants remained to them afterwards he infers a little rain in Palestine, enough for milk and flesh but not for corn.

Calvin opens on the largest scale, providence being in itself a labyrinth whose admirable method shines only when the issue of things is connected with their beginnings, explains the idiom of looking one upon another as an inactivity in which each waits for the other, and makes the journey a proof of filial reverence; Gill allows either sight of men passing with corn or common report for Jacob's learning of it, and marks that the ten are called not Jacob's sons, which they were, but Joseph's brethren.

Clarke states the rule that in Hebrew one sense is put for another, so that seeing here means learning, and notes that famines were frequent before agriculture was well understood, Canaan being peculiarly vexed in Abraham's time, in Isaac's, and now in Jacob's; Wesley says he saw the corn his neighbours had brought home.

Henry notes that all three patriarchs met famine in the land promised them, to try their faith and to wean them from this world, expands the standing into five kinds — desponding, disputing, deliberating, slumbering and delaying — and observes that they went down themselves rather than sending servants, so that none should think himself too great to take pains.

debates.question: How did Jacob learn that there was corn in Egypt?

positions.view: By ordinary means — the caravan trade, neighbours returning with corn, or common report, the Hebrew putting one sense for another
By revelation of the Holy Spirit, the opinion of some Jewish writers

outliers.claim: Records from Jarchi the opinion of some Jewish writers that Jacob perceived the corn in Egypt by revelation of the Holy Spirit rather than by report.
Infers from the survival of the flocks and servants that a little rain still fell in Palestine — enough for milk and flesh, but not for corn.

themes: Now when Jacob saw that there was corn in Egypt, Jacob said unto his sons, Why do ye look one upon another?
And he said, Behold, I have heard that there is corn in Egypt: get you down thither, and buy for us from thence; that we may live, and not die.
And Joseph’s ten brethren went down to buy corn in Egypt.
But Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, Jacob sent not with his brethren; for he said, Lest peradventure mischief befall him.
And the sons of Israel came to buy corn among those that came: for the famine was in the land of Canaan.

6.pericope_label: Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him: ye are spies

schools.summary: Ellicott explains that Joseph sold by deputy, so that only a party this large would be reported to the governor in person, sets the charge of spying in Egypt's standing distrust of the Semitic race and its frontier fortresses, glosses the nakedness of the land as its want of garrisons, and says swearing by the king's life was ordinary in antiquity and forbidden only by Gospel morality; Keil and Delitzsch quote Gerhard, that since spying was capital it is unlikely a father would expose so many sons to death at once.

Calvin joins Joseph's honour to his fidelity, holds that the conspiracy against the celestial decree was fruitless, allows two just causes for the severity — to regain Benjamin and to sift them lest a premature disclosure add a new crime — yet will not excuse the dissimulation, and finds in the oath the profane adulation of the Egyptian court; Gill assigns the failure to recognise him to twenty-two years, a grown beard, princely dress and the Egyptian tongue, and notes that the three days ended with no brother willing to carry such news home.

Clarke traces the title to the root behind the Arabic sultan, marks the irony that the precautions taken to void the dream fulfilled it, glosses the charge as footmen or trampers who buy corn while learning whether a land is defenceless enough to plunder, observes that Joseph took exactly the precautions of a stranger with every reason for suspicion, and denies that there is any oath here at all, faulting the translators.

Henry denies revenge and assigns three ends — to enrich the dreams, to bring them to repentance, and to learn the family's state, which he asked as a judge because he could not ask as a friend without discovering himself — reads the three days' ward as God humbling under a spirit of bondage those he designs for honour, and calls the formula the courtier's oath, more than yea and nay and therefore of evil.

debates.question: Is 'By the life of Pharaoh' an oath, and is Joseph blameable for it?

positions.view: No oath at all; the translators erred, since the brothers themselves report it as a solemn protest
An ordinary ancient formula, forbidden only by the stricter morality of the Gospel
The courtier's oath, learned at court, more than yea and nay and therefore of evil
An obtestation rather than an oath, yet stained by the profane adulation of the Egyptian court

debates.question: Why did Joseph deal roughly with his brethren?

positions.view: Not revenge: to fulfil the dreams, to bring them to repentance, and to learn his family's state
To regain Benjamin and to sift them, though the dissimulation itself cannot be excused
He was obliged to prove them, and did nothing they did not deserve

outliers.claim: Refuses to let Joseph's dissimulation be drawn into a precedent, treating it as a fault which human infirmity committed and divine mercy alone forgave.

themes: And Joseph was the governor over the land, and he it was that sold to all the people of the land: and Joseph’s brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth.

And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly unto them; and he said unto them, Whence come ye? And they said, From the land of Canaan to buy food.
And Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.
And Joseph remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them, and said unto them, Ye are spies; to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.
And they said unto him, Nay, my lord, but to buy food are thy servants come.
We are all one man’s sons; we are true men, thy servants are no spies.
And he said unto them, Nay, but to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.
And they said, Thy servants are twelve brethren, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan; and, behold, the youngest is this day with our father, and one is not.
And Joseph said unto them, That is it that I spake unto you, saying, Ye are spies:
Hereby ye shall be proved: By the life of Pharaoh ye shall not go forth hence, except your youngest brother come hither.
Send one of you, and let him fetch your brother, and ye shall be kept in prison, that your words may be proved, whether there be any truth in you: or else by the life of Pharaoh surely ye are spies.
And he put them all together into ward three days.

18.pericope_label: We are verily guilty concerning our brother: he turned himself about from them, and wept

schools.summary: Ellicott sees the first demand softened from nine imprisoned to one, with care that they still feel him in earnest, takes the freshness of the brothers' memory as proof that their repentance was real, clears them of lying in saying 'one is not' since they plainly believed Joseph dead, and says he melted at their first word of regret and mastered it only for fear of losing Benjamin.

Calvin makes adversity God's searching of men, dissipating illusions and extorting a confession they would gladly avoid, notes that they ascended past the cause before their eyes to a remote one, prefers the sense of punishment in the ambiguous Hebrew, and defends the suspense in which the rest were sent away while refusing to let the severity become a precedent; Gill reads the change of terms on the third day as the heart yearning under the assumed face, and the weeping as a tenderness that could no longer hold the stern countenance.

Clarke reads the Hebrew as 'I also fear the gods', the article marking the Supreme Being off from the gods of Egypt, turns conscience on the reader as the instrument of salvation now or the never-dying worm hereafter, doubts whether the interpreter was needed or affected, and reports the rabbinic tradition that Simeon had bound Joseph and put him in the pit; Wesley, with Henry, guesses Simeon was chosen as the bitterest enemy or the least humbled.

Henry treats conscience as a remembrancer which time cannot outwear, since men who made light of a crime and sat down to eat bread find it laid before them twenty years after, makes affliction the means of that awakening, lets Reuben have the comfort of having been his brother's advocate, and reads the weeping as an image of God's mercies toward repenting sinners while reason still required the stranger's part.

debates.question: Why was Simeon chosen for the hostage?

positions.view: The bitterest enemy, or the least humbled of them now
Retaliation, the rabbins holding that Simeon bound Joseph and put him in the pit
The one chiefly guilty of the wrong done him
Bold and fierce by nature, as the affair of the Shechemites shows

debates.question: Is Reuben's interjection a comfort or a reproof?

positions.view: A comfort: he alone had been his brother's advocate, and may take the testimony of his conscience
A reproof: he magnifies their fault by reminding them how late their repentance is

outliers.claim: Reads the ambiguous Hebrew as naming the punishment rather than the crime, since the word covers both as the Latin piaculum does — they are deservedly refused because they refused their brother.

themes: And Joseph said unto them the third day, This do, and live; for I fear God:
If ye be true men, let one of your brethren be bound in the house of your prison: go ye, carry corn for the famine of your houses:
But bring your youngest brother unto me; so shall your words be verified, and ye shall not die. And they did so.
And they said one to another, We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear; therefore is this distress come upon us.
And Reuben answered them, saying, Spake I not unto you, saying, Do not sin against the child; and ye would not hear? therefore, behold, also his blood is required.
And they knew not that Joseph understood them; for he spake unto them by an interpreter.
And he turned himself about from them, and wept; and returned to them again, and communed with them, and took from them Simeon, and bound him before their eyes.

25.pericope_label: Restore every man’s money into his sack: what is this that God hath done unto us?

schools.summary: Ellicott distinguishes the vessels from the travelling-bag in order to overturn the common notion that the brothers went down each with one ass and one sack, reconciles their later claim to have all found their money at the lodging-place, allows that a frequented route may have had some shelter built for beasts and attendants, and reads the restored money as encouragement and a sign of good will rather than a trap; Keil and Delitzsch find the simpler motive, that it was against Joseph's nature to trade with his father and brethren for bread.

Calvin thinks Joseph feared his already impoverished father could not buy a second time, faults him for not considering the grief he would cause, asks why the brothers set God rather than the man before them as avenger and answers that one thought possessed them, and blames them for not returning to prove their innocence when the remedy lay at hand; Gill reports Jonathan and Jarchi for Levi as the one who opened his sack, and Aben Ezra for Reuben as firstborn.

Clarke identifies the vessels with the leather-lined baskets Chardin found still in use across Asia, derives the English sack straight from the Hebrew, explains that only one found his money because in his bag alone it lay at the mouth, warns that our word inn gives a false idea of a desert halting-place, and renders their heart failing as their heart going out, the spasm of a sudden fright; Wesley supplies their reasoning, that a people who abhorred a Hebrew, having charged them as spies, must be picking a quarrel.

Henry alone reads the restored money typologically, Christ like Joseph giving out supplies without money and without price and the poorest invited to buy, while guilty consciences take good providences in a bad sense and put wrong meanings on the very things that make for them.

debates.question: Why did Joseph have their money put back in their sacks?

positions.view: As encouragement and a sign of secret good will, since fear would have kept them from returning with Benjamin
Because it was against his nature to trade with his father and brethren for bread
Because he feared his impoverished father could not buy a second time
As a figure of Christ, who gives out supplies without money and without price

outliers.claim: Faults Joseph for want of consideration: the restored money brought his father very great grief, though he had meant to relieve his poverty.
Calls absurd the common assumption that each brother travelled with a single ass and a single sack, blaming the uniform translation of three distinct words — vessel, wallet and sack.

themes: Then Joseph commanded to fill their sacks with corn, and to restore every man’s money into his sack, and to give them provision for the way: and thus did he unto them.
And they laded their asses with the corn, and departed thence.
And as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the inn, he espied his money; for, behold, it was in his sack’s mouth.
And he said unto his brethren, My money is restored; and, lo, it is even in my sack: and their heart failed them, and they were afraid, saying one to another, What is this that God hath done unto us?

29.pericope_label: Me have ye bereaved of my children: ye shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave

schools.summary: Ellicott finds the brothers' report edited, Simeon's bonds and the harsher usage suppressed lest Jacob refuse to send Benjamin, calls it irrational to read Reuben's offer literally though feeble talk all the same, and sees a man looking forward without hope who clings to Benjamin because Rachel had seemed to live on in Joseph, the father's grief having softened the brothers so that they bear the favoured child no grudge; Keil and Delitzsch take the pledge at face value as the greatest and dearest offer a son could make a father.

Calvin defends the long repetition as showing how strenuously they pleaded for leave to take the youngest, measures their fright by the fact that no one had looked in his own sack, faults Joseph for the grief the restored money caused, hears anger rather than open accusation in Jacob's complaint, and names the deepest burden — that with no hope but the promised seed, and sons from whom no blessing could be looked for, Jacob had to keep believing he cherished a Church of which scarcely any appearance was left; Gill unfolds the refusal phrase by phrase, the Targums all reading the mischief as death.

Clarke gives the Hebrew as 'all these things are upon me', loads that hasten his death and are more than he can bear, adds his doctrine of restitution — that God pardons the penitent but exacts restitution in the course of his providence, so that the binder is bound in his turn and conscience supplies the want of prison, jailer and bonds — and borrows Dodd's picture of the venerable father pleading with Benjamin at his side.

Henry turns the cry over, since it proved otherwise and all these things were for him and working together for his good, and finds distrust in the refusal, Jacob having never seen Joseph after leaving him with his brothers: it is bad with a family when children behave so that parents cannot trust them.

debates.question: How should Reuben's offer of his two sons be judged?

positions.view: The greatest and dearest offer a son could make to a father
Strange, but proof of an honest and affectionate heart
Foolish, as if the death of two grandsons could satisfy for the death of a son
Not meant literally, only a strong assurance — but feeble talk, of a piece with his general weakness
A pledge made necessary because they lay under suspicion over Joseph

outliers.claim: Draws from the chapter a doctrine of restitution — God pardons the penitent but exacts restitution through his providence — and applies it to the brothers, now captives in their turn.

themes: And they came unto Jacob their father unto the land of Canaan, and told him all that befell unto them; saying,
The man, who is the lord of the land, spake roughly to us, and took us for spies of the country.
And we said unto him, We are true men; we are no spies:
We be twelve brethren, sons of our father; one is not, and the youngest is this day with our father in the land of Canaan.
And the man, the lord of the country, said unto us, Hereby shall I know that ye are true men; leave one of your brethren here with me, and take food for the famine of your households, and be gone:
And bring your youngest brother unto me: then shall I know that ye are no spies, but that ye are true men: so will I deliver you your brother, and ye shall traffick in the land.
And it came to pass as they emptied their sacks, that, behold, every man’s bundle of money was in his sack: and when both they and their father saw the bundles of money, they were afraid.
And Jacob their father said unto them, Me have ye bereaved of my children: Joseph is not, and Simeon is not, and ye will take Benjamin away: all these things are against me.
And Reuben spake unto his father, saying, Slay my two sons, if I bring him not to thee: deliver him into my hand, and I will bring him to thee again.

And he said, My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he is left alone: if mischief befall him by the way in the which ye go, then shall ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.
